utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we'll ask the registrar to produce the various documents. If you would like to announce that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order, the additional photograph used with picture number 3 on the registry page number 02115539 will be 636, tab 1. Tab 2 would be the additional graph similar to the graph on registry page number 02115536 of the expert report. Tab 3, Your Honours, would be the new graph titled relief of direction of flight. Tab 4 will be graph that identifies the distribution of the fragments. And tab 5 will be the photocopy of the X-ray of the projectile. Tab 5 will be the photocopy of the X-ray of the projectile. And tab 6, Your Honours, will be the picture of the mortar. Defence exhibit -- the diagram of the vehicle will be Defence Exhibit 230, and the sketch showing the damage on the asphalt will be Defence Exhibit 231, Your Honours. Excuse me. Yes, Your Honours. The diagram of the vehicle will be Defence Exhibit 232, and the sketch showing damage on the asphalt will be Defence Exhibit 233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Call the next witness. Yes. Can you deal with any matters we have to cover, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: There are no protective measures for this particular witness, Your Honour. No, there are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So the Prosecution would call Kerim Mesanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. When the witness is ready, let him make the objection in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has already given evidence in the Brdjanin and the Kvocka trials. So his transcripts have already been admitted by 92 bis (D). So I kindly ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, did you give evidence in the Brdjanin and the Kvocka trials before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Could I kindly ask Your Honours that these transcripts be exhibited? They have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 638, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: The witness's evidence concerns the municipality of Prijedor, and I shall read a brief summary to the Court of that evidence. The witness grew up in Prijedor with his family and remained there until 1992. Although he is a Muslim, his wife is a Serb. Prior to the conflict, he worked in the Mobilisation Department of the secretariat for the People's Defence which was in the same building as the police. Prior to 1991, the mobilisation orders used to come from Sarajevo via Banja Luka. However, after 1991, they came from Knin in Croatia. Around the same time, the organisation of the old Territorial Defence was changed with the creation of a new federal organ referred to as a VTO, which had control over all military matters in Prijedor. This new TO structure was headed by Serbs. The Mobilisation Department became a part of the VTO, but the witness believes that he was excluded because he was a Muslim. In September and October of 1991, the witness was instructed by the chief of the VTO to provide him with lists for mobilisation containing the names of Serbs only. The units mobilised included the Banja Luka rocket unit and the 5th Kozara Brigade and the 43rd Motorised Brigade. In early 1992, weapons were secretly distributed to Serb civilians, and in February 1992, the commander of the Prijedor War Brigade was JNA Major Radmilo Zeljaja who said that he was going to level Kozarac. The Serbs established their own separate Assembly in March and took over power in Prijedor on 30th of April, 1992. Gradually the Muslims were sacked from their jobs and replaced by Serbs. On the 23rd of May, the village of Hambarine was shelled and attacked by Serb forces and shortly thereafter Serb forces attacked Kozarac. The witness was told by a colleague that the Stari Grad part of Prijedor, which is almost entirely inhabited by Muslims, was attacked and destroyed by Serbs using tanks, and they started by destroying the mosque. At that time, Simo Drljaca was head of the Prijedor police who gave the witness a freedom of movement pass. On the 24th of June, the witness was arrested by the police and placed in the cell at SUP, and whilst being removed to the Omarska camp was beaten and had four teeth knocked out. At that time, Dr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff, and the Omarska camp had been set up by Simo Drljaca on the orders of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia Ministry of Interior. The witness was detained in Omarska for about 3 months from June 1992 to August 1992. He was never charged with any offence and was never told why he was taken there. Approximately 3.000 people were detained at Omarska at any one time. Initially he was placed in the white house for the first three days of his detention, with 45 others. Those others had been badly beaten, and it was difficult to recognise them because they had blood all over them. The walls were splattered in blood. The witness helped carry a dead man out who had been beaten to death. Zeljko Meakic was in charge of the camp whilst Ranko Mijic was in charge of interrogators. According to the witness, Mijic was the most responsible for the killings and beatings which occurred at Omarska since he made the categorisation lists which were given to Meakic for implementing the beatings and killings. The actual killings and beatings were carried out by the guards on Meakic's orders. The witness, since his family was related to Meakic, only spent three days in the white house, after which Meakic ordered him to be taken to the glass house where, according to Meakic, he could guarantee his safety. Whilst in Omarska, the sleeping and sanitation conditions were inadequate. The detainees did not have enough to eat. They were often beaten on their way to meals and many were afraid even to risk leaving their cells to go and eat. They were afraid of being beaten. Whilst the witness was in Omarska, he was permanently scared of being beaten or killed. After interrogation the detainees were placed in three categories. According to the witness category 1 was the worst category to be in, since these people were to be iced. The second category would be imprisoned and the third category were meant to be released. Category 1 generally consisted of the intellectual or wealthy segment of the Muslim society in Prijedor at that time. Category 2 were people who had supported the SDA, and those in category 3 were Muslims who hadn't been involved in anything. A number of those in category 1 disappeared and were never seen again. They were taken to the Red House where the witness assumes they were killed. On one particular occasion, a hundred people who had been brought to Omarska after the cleansing of the Brdo area of Prijedor were placed in the white house and were shot during the night. In the morning, the witness saw lorries being loaded from piles of dead bodies. The Brdo area encompasses the villages of Hambarine, Biscani, and Jugovci. The witness heard, after his release, that on or around the same day about 150 men were also killed at the Keraterm camp. Whilst he was at Omarska, the witness remembers on one occasion a delegation of important people visiting. These people included Brdjanin, Zupljanin, Drljaca and Stakic who had police and other bodies guards. The witness on his release was taken to Trnopolje camp where he was detained for only one day. He then returned to Meakic's village where he lived, but again left there because of threats made against him. Now, that is a very brief summary of the witness's evidence, and with the permission of the Court, I'd like to ask the witness one or two oral questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Witness, you say that the Serb authority came into power on Prijedor on the 30th of April. Before 30th of April, how many armed attacks had the Muslims carried out against Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not one. Not one armed attack on the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: You also mention this word that people in category 1 were supposed to be "iced"? What do you mean by this word "iced"?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is I myself was on that same list on the 2nd of April to be put on ice. I just know what the driver told me. I know his nickname. What he said was, "You're lucky, because you were supposed to be iced yourself." So I suppose that means dead, icy cold dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, before the takeover on 30th of April, you say you'd been living in Prijedor. Did you know a person called Darko Mrdja?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not well, just by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Did you see him at all whilst you were in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him on the last day, which was the 6th of August when they escorted the buses to Manjaca. Him and another young guy whose nickname was Baki. He was in Prijedor. I knew him as a sportsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And were they -- was Mr. Mrdja working and Mr. Baki working for any particular organisation or body?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by that. You mean before the war or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, when you saw him at Omarska, was he a civilian? Was he in the military?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Well, he was in the military, a special unit or an Intervention Platoon. That's what they said. Although Baki wasn't a military-able man. He didn't do his military service. He was one of the once people in command on that APC which arrived on the 6th of August, arrived in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, and that would complete the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Aga, before we go on, let me clarify about the content of the Exhibit 638. You are submitting only the transcript or you are going to submit all the package with these exhibits? I cannot confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: We are wanting to submit all the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you haven't produced even an index of them. I don't know what's included in that package.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. There is no index included there, but we will make one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: -- for the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, do that so that we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we have one hour for you to examine this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I'll do my best to ask a number of relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesanovic, you've just said that the Serbs took over on the 30th of April, took over power in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they took over power without a single bullet being shot?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was no violence, nobody was injured, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not that night, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the area with majority Muslim population was placed under the control of the militia made up of Muslims and some Croats, and also under the control of the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, Kozarac, which is where there was a large armed Muslim formation in place, and then Hambarine, Biscani, et cetera, all that remained under Muslim control, did it not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, was the immediate cause for the takeover a telegram which the head of the public security station whose name was I think Hashim Talundzic --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Talundzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of police in Prijedor, and this telegram was sent by Alija Delimustafic, the Minister asking for action to be taken to block the barracks, seize the weapons from the JNA and similar acts, and that by mistake it came into the hands of the Serbs in Prijedor too. Do you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked in the Secretariat for National Defence and not in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that dispatch was sent on the 30th -- or, rather on the 29th of April, and on the 30th they took over the main institutions. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs took control on the 30th in the morning at around 5.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this telegram being tendered? The date is the 29th of April, and it is signed by the Ministry of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic, and it states the following, that a blockade should be effected of military facilities, et cetera, and that the columns of the former JNA should be prevented from leaving the barracks and communicating on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that combat action should be organised and affected throughout the territory of the BiH and that this action should be coordinated by the headquarters of Territorial Defence, the region, the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory within the frameworks of planning combat action to plan protective measures for the population, its property and so on, material goods, et cetera. Massive obstruction on all roads in Bosnia-Herzegovina on which the units of the former JNA would start to withdraw their equipment and materiel, et cetera, et cetera. So in Prijedor, everything was quiet. This telegram was sent on the 29th, ordering combat action and attacks on the army, that the barracks be blocked, et cetera, and then the Serbian Territorial Defence assumes control of Prijedor; is that right? Are the dates correct?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The dates are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness see this document. If the witness would care to look at that and make any comment about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see some dates here, the 11th of May, 1992, and that's been written in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the date of the telegram itself, which is dated the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You can see that in the upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It says the 29th of the fourth month.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Give the witness the opportunity if he wants to make any comment, do so, but if not, just hand them in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I heard this part where it says: "Pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number so-and-so, of the 27th of April, 1992, with respect to the withdrawal of the JNA units from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and because of the violations of this order of the Presidency and the expropriation and looting of property belonging to Bosnia-Herzegovina by the former JNA, I hereby order the following." I think that paragraph is essential. That goes before the order itself, why this order was actually issued in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you mean that the JNA pulling out its equipment is looting Bosnia-Herzegovinan property?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the JNA too, so it was my property too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, if that's the explanation, we needn't belabour that point any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the document be handed in to us to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, to make a clarification for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, just give the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence diagram of the vehicle will be Defence Exhibit 231. The Defence sketch showing damage on the asphalt will be Defence Exhibit 232, and this document, Your Honour, the telegram dated the 29th of April, 1992, will be Defence Exhibit 233 for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the Prosecution be provided with a copy of that document to be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's only been marked in the usual way for identification, and you will have a copy of it and indeed, can comment on it in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if the registrar can later check the number of statement of Stakic and the letter or dispatch which was shown to the same witness. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We noted a moment ago that areas with a majority Muslim population remained under the control of the police consisting of Muslims, and we mentioned Kozarac, Hambarine, Biscani, Carakovo. Is it true that at Hambarine several members of the then-already existing Army of Republika Srpska were killed on the 19th of May? No, the 22nd of May, at a checkpoint manned by the Muslims? These were soldiers who were going by unarmed, they were on their way home to Ljubija. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of Radio Prijedor, these soldiers were armed, and they provoked the incident at the checkpoint, and it was under the control of policeman Aziz Aliskovic. That is what the shooting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that is when four of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not four, one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I know from Prijedor. That was the first shot fired on the 22nd of May in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the killer is also known; right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this Aziz that you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Aziz was the command of the checkpoint, Aziz Aliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was in command of the people who killed this soldier?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say, according to my information, four were killed. But let us go back to you and your testimony in writing. You were working in the mobilisation department of the municipal Secretariat for National Defence in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you stayed in that position until the 22nd of June, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you remained in that position even after the Serbs took over power on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: With a break since mid-May when we were all dismissed, and then I was called back to work in June. Just before I left to Omarska, because they couldn't find an adequate replacement for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that six out of seven Muslims from your service remained in the job after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Until mid-May. Only Becir Medunjanin didn't come to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So only Becir Medunjanin was replaced.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know why he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the SDA, and he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, we found that out of seven Muslims, six remained on duty and that one was Medunjanin. Do you know that in the military Tribunal in Banja Luka there were proceedings against him and he was accused of having organised and participated with some others like Muhamed Cehajic, Mujadzic Mirsad, Hasan Talundzic, that he had participated in the procurement of weapons, the formation of paramilitary units and prevented weapons being returned to the legal authorities?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here is the indictment. He was not replaced because he was a Muslim. He is the only one who was replaced out of you -- seven of you, and here is the indictment against him and the others relating to these acts that I mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to tender this into evidence. Not because he was a Muslim but because he committed a criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 5th of September, 1992, an indictment after he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crnkic, my former teacher, was killed. Aliskovic Aziz was killed. Cehajic Muhamed was killed, Medunjanin Becir was killed. That is as far as I know. And the indictment was issued on the 5th of the September, whereas we were killed in the month of June. So this is an indictment against dead people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. If you'd hand that in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that prior to an indictment certain acts have to be done regarding the crime for which the indictment is issued?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: But Becir Medunjanin's top of the head was cut off, and his chest was wounded. So I don't know that such acts need to precede an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I couldn't have committed those acts as a dead person?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: My opinion was he was killed first and then indicted because the indictment is dated September and he was killed in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think one needs to read the whole document. It isn't a lengthy one. I wouldn't dwell on it. Their Honours will be able to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We'll mark the next document for identification. We will then decide if it has any relevance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence Exhibit 235, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesanovic, is it true that no one forced you during that time to sign any kind of loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 2 of your statement, it is a statement the 4th of February, 1999, that no one forced you to sign an oath of allegiance.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That is true. I said it was offered, but I didn't sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your colleague in the department was Stjepan Maric, a Bosnian Croat, Maric was sent to Manjaca in 1991 because he didn't carry out the order on mobilisation? This is also in your statement.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Maric worked for the defence as -- department as a computer expert. He went to Manjaca as a head of a regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is the following true in your statement which may -- that he had produced some false software programmes? He wasn't sent to prison because he was a Croat but because he had committed some crimes?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He received a hundred thousand marks personally from Mr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that sounds rather unbelievable, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say on page 2, paragraph 3, that people in Prijedor were against the order on mobilisation taken at the federal level?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Which mobilisation? Which year and which month?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 3 you speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the witness kindly be provided with a copy of his statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why? Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: So that he can see the parts which he's actually alleged to have said and comment upon them. It's more easy for him to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in those days, and we're talking about 1991 still, didn't Yugoslavia still exist as a unified state and that decisions by the federal authorities were legal?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the hierarchy applied differed. It went Belgrade, Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Prijedor. That is why we were opposed, because the orders were coming from Knin, written in Cyrillic from Knin, which did not correspond to any system of the country we had before the war. We were under the military district of Banja Luka, and above Banja Luka was Sarajevo, and above Sarajevo, Belgrade, and that is why we opposed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that in the spring of 1991, the last regular mobilisation of territorial units was carried out?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say when they distributed weapons they gave Serbs automatic rifles and Muslims, M48-rifles.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That was true. That applied to the TO detachment mobilised at Urije. Serbs received automatic rifles. Members of the Muslim ethnicity received M-48s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you actually see that and you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't mobilised. I was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were not mobilised and you did not receive a rifle.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I worked in the national defence secretariat. I carried out the mobilisation. I apologise, Your Honour, for speaking so fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say things started to change drastically after 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us why?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Because drunken soldiers were coming back from the Croatian battlefront with insignia which were insulting and provocative of the non-Serbs. They were wearing cockades, White Eagles patches, patches with the four Ss. I don't know whom they belonged to. They did what they wanted around town. They drank and ate without paying for it. They broke cafes up, and that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were working in the national defence, was there a JNA unit there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Prijedor, as such, did not have any active military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the situation deteriorated after the proclamation on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: And even before. In November 1991, there was some shooting. There was a carpet of bullets in the streets when they returned from the Croatian front. Things worsened around the 4th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what about the well-known statements by Alija Izetbegovic on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina? When were they made? Was it before the 4th of November or after that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Statements, yes. But these were just statements. There were statements by Karadzic that one people would disappear from the face of the earth too. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You know that the formation of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina was the aspiration of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Of the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with the Izetbegovic's statement that peace would be sacrificed for an independent Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Reactions to all this started in November; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We had a mobilisation before that of the reserve forces and sending them to Croatia. Strange things were happening. The Muslims didn't go to the Croatian front either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mesanovic. Now, tell me, please, what do you know about the organisation of paramilitary units in those days by the Patriotic League and other paramilitary formations of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to answer that question because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you do know, for instance, that at the time of the events you are testifying about, there were several thousand armed members of Muslim forces in Kozarac, for instance?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they were that many. There was a TO unit of Kozarac, but they didn't number several thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was information about this.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply I don't know that, because those were the Territorial Defence. I was in the civilian Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the formation of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't involved for a moment, and I had no knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about the collection of weapons as announced by Radio Prijedor. I'm aware of the proclamations to hand in side weapons, personal weapons, including pistols. Everything needed to be handed in. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about the arming, not the disarming.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about the arming of Serbs in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you don't know anything about the arming of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Prijedor, and I didn't live in the surrounding villages, so I don't know that. And I know that weapons were distributed publicly even to children in Prijedor in the spring of 1992. And I also think that there is a figure as to how many weapons were seized from the Muslims. I think this was a hundred or so. I saw the data in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you're talking about the arming of Serbs, were they arming themselves for the purpose of self-defence or for some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was -- it proved to be for some other reasons because they had no need for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw this dispatch from Alija Delimustafic. How can you say that they had no need to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think the area in which I lived there was that no need for an indication of a need for self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it was peaceful until the dispatch arrived ordering attacks on the military. Tell me, now can this function, as you just explained, that you started receiving orders via Knin?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can't explain that. Maybe you can explain it because you were in the top leadership at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that that is not true. That is why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I could say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you say that by order of the federal government all the weapons were taken from the local offices of the TO and placed under JNA control.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the TO staffs were abolished and the weapons were taken over by military territorial bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that on the 29th of May, 1990, so this was prior to any kind of conflict, the 29th of May, of 1990, a decision was taken by the Presidency of Yugoslavia on the takeover of weapons and military equipment of the TO and their storage in JNA warehouses, precisely to avoid uncontrolled use of such weapons and this applied to the whole of Yugoslavia, that all the republics of Yugoslavia had to do this, and they did?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And after that Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia happened. Once the weapons were taken from TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were not taken, they were placed under JNA control, and this happened in Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You call it what you like. I didn't even have an official pistol. It was taken away from me in 1992. It was a 7.62 millimetre pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the -- working in the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not delivered a part of the weapons that should have been delivered to it?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have an active military in Prijedor, only the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there was a barracks?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were no conscripts there, only the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And these officers didn't engage in any kind of wartime activities. It was a commission that should have taken over the weapons following orders of the Presidency of the SFRY. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was not a commission. The barracks always had a certain number of active-duty officers who made up the staff of the unit that was being established for a certain purpose. So it wasn't a commission of any kind. They were just people there who were there parallelly. They had the same function, organisationally speaking, as I did in the civilian section. The regiment commander was the barracks commander at that time, and all the other administrative employees, finance and so on, that was something else. But there were no soldiers. When I say "soldiers," I mean the young men doing their military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that the Party of Democratic Action and Izetbegovic himself at the beginning of 1991 made the decision that Muslims should not go to the JNA and that he called all the soldiers and officers born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, appealed to them to leave the JNA and also prevented further recruitment of the JNA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know about an order not to respond to the reserve force and not to respond to mobilisation so that they shouldn't be sent to the front in Croatia. I know about that. Now, we regularly enrolled in the JNA up to a certain month but not afterwards. I can't remember the exact time. After what went on in Croatia, they were no longer sent to the JNA and Croatia and Bosnia and Slovenia, I think, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party, through its representatives appealed to the Muslims of Prijedor not to respond to the appeal launched by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I wasn't a member of the Party of Democratic Action at all, the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know about their appeal?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you about that either. I know there were rumours to that effect. Now, whether it was the party's official position, I can't say because I wasn't a member of that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that on the 12th of April, 1992, Alija Izetbegovic ordered an all-out attack on JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. While you were working in Prijedor, you say on page 3 of your statement, the last paragraph, up until the 22nd of May, nothing was going on in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Except for what happened on the 4th of May, I think, and that was the killing -- the killing that took place in Dubica when three Muslims were taken out of a regular bus line and this man was killed, and after that a curfew was enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is borne out by my information too. It was linked to the killing of a soldier on the previous day, and then somebody out of retaliation killed those three Muslims, and in order to prevent further violence, a curfew was introduced which applied to everyone. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I was concerned, I didn't go out. I don't know whether it applied to everybody, though, because you could hear shooting after 10.00 p.m., and songs were sung, cafes were open, and underneath my own window there was an all-night cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now since you're talking about the stay in Omarska and you say that the white house was reserved for people from Kozarac, all those who had taken part in the attack on Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was an attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what they said. Because the question was why was I in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that too. Didn't you confirm a moment ago that on the 22nd of May there was a killing that took place at the -- at a checkpoint by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that one man was killed, but my information tells me that four soldiers were killed, and of those four, two were Croats and two were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The on-site investigation was conducted by the Serbs, so the reports are drafted as befits that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, we're not talking about an on-site investigation. That's not the point. But the point is the document that I have in my possession, perhaps you're going to say that somebody was accused and charged after he was killed. And this is an official report that said that Amer Ceric was apprehended. The 10th of June, 1992, is the date. And then it goes on to say that in the village of Hambarine, two uniformed Serbs were killed who were passing by in a car together with two Croats who were wounded. And then it goes on to say,"Dado told me that the man was killed by someone called Siki and that his real surname was Sikiric because he stopped a soldiers' patrol in Hambarine." And there's a lengthy statement to follow which speaks about the whole event, and I think that it can be tendered into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness see it first. Yes. If the witness would take a brief look at that and whether he can assist us or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Amer Ceric was killed. His father is Jusuf and works in the Nafta gas company. And the name rang a bell but, yes, he was killed after the statement. Mesic Halil, killed in Omarska, and he was going to make a film about the attack on Prijedor. He was killed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed one man and who killed the other? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Who killed them all. But Amir and Halim and Muhamed and all the rest of them. Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the Muslim attack on Prijedor, according to what a witness said here before you, 17 Serb policemen were killed. So who killed them?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you who killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I assume you know that they were killed, because they were buried.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They were policemen mostly from Bosanski Novi. Do you know that? That most of the policemen were from Bosanski Novi? Now, what were they doing in Prijedor on that morning and where were they killed? Were they killed in Prijedor or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Mesanovic, as far as my information tells me, they were killed during the Muslim attack on Prijedor, and you say you lived in Prijedor throughout and that you knew about the attack?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear shooting that morning, and it went on until noon. And amongst them was my uncle with two of his sons. One of them is in Australia and the other is in Switzerland. The house was razed to the ground. It is across the road from Radio Prijedor on the pretext that the attack came from this house and that it was launched by my uncle and two sons, and he doesn't know about the whereabouts of his first son because it was a son from a first marriage, but it is true that the house no longer exists and it used to be across the road from Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the house destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: It was destroyed during the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the attack on Prijedor was conducted by Muslim forces, was it not?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. And my uncle was not in Prijedor at the time, and the Tribunal can check that out. When my uncle and his son left for Switzerland and when the first son disappeared and is probably living in Australia but he haven't heard from him for 30 years. So official police reports say that my uncle and the two sons worked in Prijedor, which is not true, and the house was razed to the ground, and there were two shops underneath it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When those soldiers were killed at the checkpoint, do you know that in fact, Aziz Aliskovic and Crljenkovic, Sikiric, Ferid, and the others were there and Mujadzic, Mirsad and Esef Crnkic joined them later, as well as Husein Crkic, Jasmin Beharolic [phoen], Husa Pasic, Emir Paltak and others.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I don't know who came. I just heard that Aziz Aliskovic was there but I don't know about the others. I think he was from Biscani or Jugovci or somewhere like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's time now for an adjournment. Before we do, do you want the witness to produce this document or other that you referred to? Do you want it produced? Do you want it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, produced it. Very well. We'll give it the next number for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D236, Your Honours, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes. We will remind the witness, Mr. Mesanovic, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, please. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes left, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll do my best to use them rationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the killing at the checkpoint that the Muslim forces did not want to hand over the killers and that an appeal was made for them to hand over the perpetrators of the crime? The appeal was made over the radio.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that that happened. All I know was that they asked weapons to be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the army took action only afterwards because they wanted to block off that checkpoint, not to prevent any repetitions?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two tanks of the Intervention Platoon from the Zarko Zrenjanin barracks passed by that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean after the killing at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that two days after this event, that is to say on the 24th of May, in Jakupovici from a military checkpoint the army was sent off and that the military column was shot at?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The same as in Hambarine, the cause for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a certain Zeljaja who threatened to raze Kozarac to the ground. Is that a man from your local area? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: From the surrounds of Sarajevo. And he came to replace Bosko Divljak [phoen] to organise mobilisation and organisation with the platoon. I think he was captain first class and later received the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the main road from Banja Luka to Prijedor was blocked for a length of 15 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the checkpoint was set up by members of the Patriotic League and the TO and the 3rd of May, 1992, as early as that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: The checkpoint was in Kozarac. I don't know where else it could have been. After Kozarac, you have Serb villages, Lamovita, Omarska, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And all that was blocked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but the -- that's what the Serb authorities said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that Sead Cirkin organised an attack on the military column and he was the commander of the Green Berets in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in Jakupovici the Muslims killed a soldier named Zgonjanin with a sniper and set fire to a tank?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the fighting went on for two days?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is true then?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: What is true is that they used multiple barrel rocket launchers for two days to fire and if you respond with a shell when a bullet is fired, then that's not a proper fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But the Muslims attacked on the 30th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at Kurevo and Carakovo, Captain Muhic, Suad Halilovic, Kemo Alagic, and Slavko Acimovic prepared and trained men and devised a tactical attack for Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that Acimovic was killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that the group of Alagic, Kemo, and Suadic nicknamed Suhi had the task of attacking from the bridge and attacking the motel.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Slavko Acimovic's group under the command of Captain Muhic attacked the building and assumed control of the town?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in the group for me to be able no know what assignments who had, nor did I take part in the perpetration of any plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that from the direction of Puharska, for example, where the 4th group started out to take over the bypass that a young man was killed there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the commander of the group whose name was Kemo Alagic and his nickname was Divljak?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that the 3rd group was commanded by man called Rizvanovic and the fourth by Izet Mesic, Hadzija?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew Hadzija by sight but I don't know which group he commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to you, how many Serb policemen were killed on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the number you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, do you know that a group of -- a group escaped towards Sredici [phoen], Biscani, Kalajevo, and Donja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that group, the one that secretly dispersed, were given the task of resting up and three days later on the 2nd of June too have a meeting in Studenac near Sisin Hrast [phoen] or Kurevo in order to ascertain the plans of attack on Ljubija and the police station there?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself were arrested on the 24th of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't leave my house until the 15th or 16th of June. I didn't dare leave my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were apprehended by a policeman what's surname was Kovacevic whom you knew from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you he was arresting you because somebody who had been arrested mentioned you in one of their statements and this was to be checked out?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were first of all put up at that so-called white house and then were you were transferred to the staklenik [phoen], the glass house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Meakic transfer you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic told you that the statement you gave during your interrogations was not a good one and that you ought to amended it?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Meakic wanted to help you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that Meakic was the commander of the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, you know that that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, that is correct. That is correct, sir. And you forgot to say something. Zeljko Meakic had family ties with me. We were family; my brother married his sister. So Zeljko was the commander throughout the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to my information, he couldn't have been commander because there were people who were senior to him. He might have been in command of the group providing security, but he wasn't the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: He was the captain, the commander of the guards who beat people, killed people and took people off for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now is it true that Meakic did not kill anyone or beat anyone or take anyone off for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything like that, but if he was the main person in command, then I see no reason why he should do that, why that would be his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. I'm saying that he wasn't the main person in command and that is a wrong piece of information.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I know two men who were there: Ranko Mijic, the head of the inspectors, and Zeljko Meakic, who was the chief. Now you can call him what you like, whether of security for the camp or the detainees, I wouldn't know, I can't say. I don't know what happened round about, whether there was any third formation there, military, civilian or whatever. Police or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. According to my information, the War Presidency of the Prijedor municipality made a decision according to which the members of the reserve police force was to be decreased to provide security for Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska to be taken over by the army but the army refused to take on the obligation of providing security for those camps. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of these people, ones that you mention in any capacity whatsoever, whether being in the police force or in those camps were people from your local area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the Prijedor municipality. I don't know all the people, but I know the people that I mentioned and Prijedor municipality, when I came to Omarska and I heard from the inmates who came before me because I came later on 24 hour -- days later in fact, and I heard from them there were groups there and the army was Banja Luka Banija or wherever. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you were released from Omarska on the 6th of August and sent to Trnopolje from which you were released on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you went home to Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that after 24 hours in Prijedor, you went to Petrov Gaj precisely to the house of the Zeljko Meakic family?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you spent the next two and a half months there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 16th or 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there together with Zeljko Meakic's family, his wife and child; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were you with then?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: With the parents of my sister-in-law, and that is Zeljko's cousin from the house across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Meakic protected you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know from what.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Meakic got a forged identity card for you?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is my sister-in-law from Novi Sad who obtained that ID for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Meakic is a relative of yours.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this emanates from page 3, paragraph 5 of your statement. A moment ago you said that you never saw Meakic hitting anyone or engaging in any kind of violence.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same applies to Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So neither Meakic nor Kvocka never hit anyone nor abused anyone or engaged in any kind of violence?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I saw and that's what I said at the trial of Kvocka and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you were wife is a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after all this suffering, you found shelter and safety in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: With a Serbian identity card that was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, if you had wanted to, couldn't you have gone to the territory under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Along which route?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Any route going through the far west of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was under Serb control. You know that well. The only route was through Serb-held territory with a false ID in Zdravko Lukic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't go to territory under Muslim control so as not to come under the mobilisation order.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never gave that a thought, because I had escaped from hell, and I was thinking of how to save my family and pull them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you did, didn't you? You went to Serbia, and you stayed in Serbia for how long?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after that you went to Germany?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: As a Serb, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know any Muslim who had problems in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned a certain Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that he was a local criminal?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe him in those terms. Zoran Zigic grew up with me in the same part of town. We were even together for our tonsils to be operated. He had his life. I have mine. Now, whether he was a criminal, I wouldn't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a document dated the 1st of July, 1992, and it says: "Instructions for the apprehension of Zoran Zigic to the prison administration in Banja Luka, public security service in Prijedor, the 1st of July, 1992, Zigic Zoran," et cetera, "from Prijedor," his address, "to be arrested because of reasonable grounds to believe that he received money, and it is in this connection that the order is issued for him to be arrested. The Secretariat of the Internal Affairs in Prijedor, public prosecutor informs under this number that he had started -- that he issued a request for investigating procedures against Zoran Zigic for the criminal act of receiving bribes. So this is a person who did engage in criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: You read that out. Zoran Zigic was a taxi driver. Why could he have received a bribe as a taxi driver?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that, but I have this document. You can have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. This was on July 1st. I was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you mentioned him in your statement?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And my question was whether he was a local criminal, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: There was a killing that he was charged with, but he was acquitted. So I can't say that he was a criminal if the court acquitted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that you received a special pass from Simo Drljaca on the basis of which you were able to move around after the curfew?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since a moment ago that you said you were not able to move around, did you move about or did you not? That is one question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And my second question, why did you receive that special pass? What were you doing? What were the activities you were engaged in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These must be the last questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did move about from my house to my work in the presence of the driver of the Secretariat of National Defence, Branko Milosevic. I needed this permission because I said I lived and grew up in that town, and everyone knew who I was, and I just had confirm that with a letter signed by Simo Drljaca, who was the big boss in Prijedor. I never moved around alone without this driver who was armed and with the presence of the head of the military territorial body, Cedomir Zitovac, who was also armed, because the computer wasn't working and we had to go to Zitopromet. And there were checkpoints all over town at which we would be stopped. If one of the local Serbs recognised me, it was necessary for me to show them this pass signed by Simo Drljaca and that I wasn't driving around for the fun of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mesanovic, you said a moment ago that via Serbia you went to Germany, and you stayed there until when?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Until I went to a third country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but you also said during the examination-in-chief that your uncle went to Australia and his children.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: One son to Australia, and my son [as interpreted] and uncle went to Switzerland in 1991. His son may have gone in 1990, but my uncle in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: They went there directly from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: They went to work there as medical technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I would like to know how many Muslims left Bosnia in the same way as you did via Serbia and went abroad.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I know that Emir Puskar used the same kind of ID card under the same name and left, because that ID card was sent back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: About the events you testified about in the camp, you said that you heard shots one night.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that that night that the fog was very thick and it lasted all night.

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Until morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Until what time?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Until about 5.00 or 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how far was the white house from where the shots were heard?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe some 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Judges, since you mentioned that that night 150 men were killed, on what basis did you come to that number?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the number that entered the white house as we counted them when they came off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who counted them?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Not just me but those of us who were in the glass house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why did you count those men?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Simply to know how many of us were there and how many had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said in your statement that, "Later when I was in Trnopolje, I learned that that night 150 men had been killed."

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm talking about Omarska, not Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And 150 were killed in Keraterm as well?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard that. Even Radio Prijedor announced that this was an escape attempt in all those camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that that night in each of those camps that many people were killed. So you're just assuming it?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there were more than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Does the Prosecution have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask the witness a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Now, according to the accused, this dispatch was received on the 29th of April and then by 5 a.m. the next morning, the Serbian authority had assumed power. Did you observe or notice anything to indicate that the Serb community were getting ready to take over power before 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: And finally, can you confirm just for clarity whether there were one or two killing incidents at camps? Were they separate instances that you mentioned at Omarska and Keraterm, or only one?

utterances.speaker: KERIM MESANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. In Omarska, as I said, that was the first time that we heard shots. And I saw the killing of Crnalic. I don't know his first name. He was killed in front of the white house. That is the only shooting that I saw and heard, but in the night between the 25th and the 26th, between Thursday and Friday, with Esad Sadikovic and another two guys, I took out Mehmedalija Sarajlic, his body, and we left him near the fence next to the red house. That is where they were killed, beaten up to death. And they would be left there for days sometimes, and then a yellow truck would take them away in the morning. We used to call it Zuco. Because if someone were to see a killing, he would just see it and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The Prosecutor's question as to whether it was known, it wasn't known except that a new parallel authority was established. That is the Serb Assembly was formed in March, before the takeover. And all the administrative bodies of the municipality existed in parallel. All the secretariats. They were -- there were all the directors who would replace the Muslims. And this was even announced on Prijedor radio, the Serbian Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let us thank the witness for coming here to give his evidence. We're grateful. It's now concluded. Mr. Mesanovic, if you would like to leave now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Dr. Ton Zwaan whose report of November 2003 has been served. He's actually just outside the door, so he can be brought in immediately. The Chamber has seen his report already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind, so it should be plain that we will hear some brief questions by the Prosecution. We allow one hearing as far as the accused is concerned. If he wishes to ask that length of question of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Aptel, who the Chamber hasn't seen before, and Mrs. Tromp, who the Chamber has seen before, will be in court, they having been involved in the preparation of this evidence. And the Chamber should also have the curriculum vitae of Dr. Zwaan, where it was served a couple of days after the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would please take his usual statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Full name, please sir?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Anthony Zwaan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Dr. Zwaan we will come to your curriculum vitae in a minute, but you're a social scientist, and is the position as follows, that you were asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to prepare a report on research into genocides and other mass crimes which target specific groups?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Such crimes or such events, if we use a neutral term, have only been capable of being described as genocide since that word was coined in the mid-twentieth century?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in fact have such events been the subject of academic study before that word was coined?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, but then other words were used like atrocities or massacres or barbarous acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since the Second World War, has there been developing interest in and research upon such events conducted by a wide range of social science and other disciplines?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct, especially since the 1980s. The field, so-called field of genocide studies has developed in which historians and social scientist are active.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you could keep your voice up a little bit although, of course, it's all amplified so we can hear you. You are now based at the recently opened centre for Holocaust studies in Amsterdam?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that centre is not unique. It's one of several or many similar centres around the world researching into these events.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With that in mind, then, very briefly your curriculum vitae which has been made available to the Court, the accused, and the amici, you set out your history since 1970 as an academic, your qualifications most recently being your doctorate in the year 2001 at Amsterdam, doctorate being in civilisation and decivilisation, studies on state formation and violence, nationalism and persecution.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You set out the other publications under your name. In the report for this Chamber, were you asked specifically to omit all reference or any reference to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to draw the report on the basis of other research, and focusing in particular on four events known as genocides in the 20th century, the Armenian, the Nazi, Rwanda, and Cambodia?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The underlying or one of the underlying interests and problems that academics in your field are concerned with is how it comes about that neighbour can land up killing neighbour, colleague, colleague, apparently in pursuit of some other objective.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to do so on a large scale?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
