utterances.text: Your study is focused by reference to earlier and other events on whether there are common characteristics that can be discerned, whether there are conclusions that can be drawn from such characteristics when they occur?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your report, and I look now at the index, is in eight sections of which the eighth is a summary of conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's always helpful for those viewing to have as good an understanding as they can of material dealt with in writing. With the Court's leave, might page 38 and 39 as appropriate, the summary, be laid on the overhead projector? And I have about one or two questions to ask per sector, and I'll link the questions to the conclusions that are to be found. If that's an acceptable course, I'd ask the usher to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first part of your report is by way of introduction, and if goes from pages 3 to 7. Nothing I need cover with you in that. Starting at page 7 and under, as it were, chapter 1 of your report, you deal with the definitions and discussions of the term genocide that has both a legal meaning, ultimately the only meaning of significance here, but has a broader use and connotation; correct?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I focused on historical and social scientist discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. At your conclusion in relation to this part, we can see on the passage on the overhead projector that you make the point that genocide and other en masse crimes targeting specific groups should be distinguished from war and civil war, although we should recognise that war or civil war may contribute to the development of genocidal processes. At page 11 of your report, and within this section, you draw to our attention the problem, if it is a problem, of the Holocaust of being the standard model. Could you just amplify that in a sentence for so for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. us?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, the murder of the Jews was the basis for drawing up the United Nations Convention, and I think because it's the case of genocide about which most people know quite something. It has become, so to speak, the model against which people measure other or new cases of genocide, and that has some advantages but also some disadvantages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The disadvantage being related to the scale of events?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Among other thing being related to the scales, yes, but I think people tend to measure, unwittingly or wittingly, new cases or other cases of genocide against the standard model, and then might easily conclude that these new cases are not really cases or are not so very serious cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although they may in fact demonstrate to the social scientist the same constellation of events and circumstances that can be found in genocides of the larger type?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yeah, I would prefer here the term similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the scale, what are some of the other factors that make the 1945 phenomenon not necessarily a good example, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that depends on what you want to argue. I think it is a very important case to study over and over again, the murder of the Jews but it is also, like every other case, a unique case with certain unique features and then there are also some similarities, and what I'm after in this report is looking for similar conditions and similar causative mechanisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be -- if I can add to His Honour's question. I don't know if you wanted to -- am I cutting across Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be in amplification of that answer and to assist His Honour you could, if it's helpful or appropriate, identify some of the characteristics of the 1945 event that are not to be found generally and are unique?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, a very important fact to my mind is that the Nazis went for the complete genocide of every Jew within the reach of the German authorities, and in other cases that does not have to be the case or is not happened -- has not happened in that way. So it was -- it was an effort at the really complete genocide, and that's one of the exceptional characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Within this same section of your report at paragraph 12, you set out a list of conditions identified by a fellow academic, Helen Fein, and it may be that the usher, as well as leaving the final page on the overhead projector, can lay on other pages from time to time, paragraph 12, coming your way. This academic identified continuity of attacks by perpetrators, collective organisation of perpetrators, victims selected by membership of a group and being defenseless in circumstances where murder is favourably sanctioned by the perpetrators as some of the identifying characteristics.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, you can use these characteristics or these criteria to look at specific cases and see whether they fit, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having identified her standard or unexceptional list, you in fact set out your report in slightly different headings, but let -- can you help us with this: Your approach, as far as you can judge it, is it within the main body of present research into these events or would it in any way be eccentric or extreme?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: No. I've done my best to formulate, let's say, the general consensus within the field with regard to conditions and processes. So I wouldn't judge it eccentric at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn, then, to part 2 of your report which starts at page 13 and goes only to page 15, headed war, civil war, and genocidal crimes. It finds its expression in your summary. Sorry. I already dealt with that summary, I think.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's one point of -- I think you think great importance to be found at paragraph 23 on page -- footnote 23 on page 14, and this is the concept of monopoly of violence and its relationship to the monopoly of taxation. Expand on that in a sentence or so, its significance for potential perpetrators and victims and then we'll look at a modern demonstrative example?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the monopoly of violence is the most central characteristic of any state and the monopoly of violence does several things. It reserves the right to use violence to the state and usually forbids it to groups of citizens. That's one aspect. Another aspect is the formal basis of public order in the sense that the forces of monopoly of violence, usually the police or military or judiciary, will take action when groups of citizens or individual citizens will take recourse to violence so the monopoly of violence is the guarantee of public order. I think I should leave --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Its relationship with the monopoly of taxation is probably obvious but a sentence on that?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, they're both closely intertwined. If you do not have a monopoly on violence you will not be able to levy taxes. And the other way around. If you don't have taxes, you are not able to pay for a monopoly of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once the monopoly of violence is broken, penetrated by other forces, disintegrates or whatever, what is the consequence for the sense of impunity in wrongdoers? What is the consequence in vulnerability for potential victims?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, if the monopoly of violence is not functioning any more or when certain groups are deliberately excluded from the protection of monopoly of violence, that will mean that some groups in society or some organisations might take recourse to violence for their own private ends. Maybe I could give as an example the functioning of the Mafia in Italy and other countries. Mafia functions there where they can take recourse to private uses of violence which a state is not able to repress or contain, and similarly, in genocidal situations, the state will not try any more to contain violence for certain political ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Countries may like to think of themselves as absolutely civilised, and the notion that they are dependent on something called or something characterised as a monopoly of violence may be unappealing, but was there example in a country that are proud of its civilisation, Canada, recently that demonstrates exactly what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes. When the police decided to go on strike there, you saw in a very short period of time a fast increase in the uses of violence and in crime. There are other another example, for instance, when the central lighting broke down in New York, as you may remember a few years ago. Looting, plundering and other criminal activities certainly increased. So I could -- if I -- if I may, I could say the civilisation of a society and also the civilised behaviour between people depends very much on the guarantee of security, and security is guaranteed by an monopoly of violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the Canadian example again, lawlessness broke out within hours, not days. Literally within hours?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Within hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Part 3 of your report from pages 15 to 17, headed crisis and genocidal crimes, finds reflection in your second conclusion in the summary to the effect that such crimes can only develop and take place under conditions of serious and enduring crisis, destabilisation -- third sentence the state concerned, polarisation processes, depacification and increasing use of violence at the heart of such crises. You address at paragraph 18 on page 15 the possibility that genocides or crimes of mass targeting of groups can erupt spontaneously from the bottom up as a normal aspect of society, and if so, what's your conclusion according to all the research?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: I think that just never happens. Genocide or genocidal crime is a very exceptional thing in a society, and it never develops from the bottom up nor out of the blue, so to speak, and that's why I've tried to argue that to understand genocidal crimes or genocidal processes you have to look at the crisis the whole society gets into before you can understand what's happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We turn now to part 4 of your report, which is between pages 17 and 21, finding expression in your conclusions in the third conclusion, which is a long and central conclusion. I'd like you to help us a little bit by expansion, perhaps, of paragraph 29, and it may be this is a paragraph the usher could just lay over the top of the conclusion for the time being, paragraph 29 on page 19. Can you link for us your conclusions about the monopoly of violence, about factual dictatorships and impunity?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to do that. Normally, the monopoly of violence is under the command of central political authorities of a society so when we have to do with situations in which genocidal crimes are developing, we must conclude that the central authorities do no longer maintain the monopoly of violence in a impersonal and lawful way, but that, in one way or another, and this make take different forms, they have given permission, directly or indirectly, to groups of perpetrators to go on with certain forms of mass crime. So there is a direct relation between the level of specification of a society and the decisions central authorities make. I don't know if I answered your question enough this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Factual dictatorships?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: It's very important for central authorities, for certain extreme decisions, that they can dispose of enough power to make such decisions. So that will mean two things. It will mean that they will try to -- to withhold restraints from their own society and also that they will also try to withhold restraints from other societies or other state governments. So they will strive after a lot of power to put it simply to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: -- to be able --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the particular events that you have considered, is there any pattern of factual or de facto dictatorships being dressed up or continuing to wear the clothing of democratic process?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: One example I could think of is the sort of referenda Hitler used to organise after he got power in 1933, in which he tried to get majority votes from the German electorate for his policies and for certain decisions. So I would say that there he tried, for instance, or the National Socialist leadership tried, to show some democratic trappings to what was already in fact already a dictatorship from the half -- halfway through 1933. That would be an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we now focus, and this is the only time that I shall focus on a paragraph in your report in detail, on paragraph 29 on the overhead projector. Picking it up at the end of paragraph 28, you say how sometimes under certain conditions - this is paragraph 28 - incidental atrocities and massacres may result, or pogroms, but normally the state and its law enforcement agencies, the police and the judiciary, and if necessary the military, will contain, repress and sanction such forms of violence. You go on to say: "When the state authorities fail to do so, or are not willing to do so, they are encouraging and contributing to the development of a genocidal process. Such processes involve large numbers of people as victims, and considerable numbers as perpetrators. That shows again the crucial importance of the central political leadership in committing genocidal crimes. Genocidal crimes are top-down affairs." From the research into the events you considered and from the learning of those and other such events, how clear are you on this top-down conclusion?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: I think I should state that we know of no case of genocide or a genocidal process in which it had grown from bottom up. I think in all cases I know of and other experts do too, you can draw the conclusion that decisions of the central political and military authorities are of decisive importance, whether a genocidal process developments, yes or no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this conclusion -- we're using the word genocide but of course the report relates to crimes, mass crimes, targeting individual groups or groups that are picked on?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's your conclusion for that type of event?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the last part of this paragraph, you say as follows: "From the researched cases of genocidal crimes in the 20th century, structural and systematic series of forceful uprooting and violent events, deportations and massacres over an extended area during an extended period of time, the conclusion can be drawn that such crimes happen with knowledge, approval, and involvement of the state authorities." Is that an amplification of the conclusion you've just given me?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that in any way reflect the availability of information in this part of the development of our world in contrast perhaps to analyses that might have to be made of medieval, late medieval, or whatever you like periods of our histories?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: If you turn to earlier periods of history, you should recognise that the structure of society was quite different from what it is now, so you should specify then the conditions of the state and the monopoly of violence at that time to understand the type of atrocities and massacres which took place, for instance, at the end of the Middle Ages or in early modern times, and they are partially different but also in these cases, I think, the decision of the highest authorities in any society are of crucial importance to understand large-scale violent crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher would be good enough to remove that sheet so we can see the conclusion of the summary paragraph, again the only one I'm going to look at in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask when you speak of the bottom up and the top down phenomena, are you speaking principally about the genesis, the start of the -- the beginning of the phenomenon? Because isn't there a stage at which the two would coincide, would merge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're partly correct, I think. Once the decision has been made that large-scale violence will not be stopped, it might be so that certain groups from bottom down see opportunities or get impunity to go on with their own mass crimes, violent crimes. Maybe I can offer you an example. When the Germans occupied the eastern part of Poland, at several locations, about 30 in all, local Polish leaders decided to organise pogroms against the Jews, but that to my mind was only possible because the German authorities, who had already initiated anti-Jewish policies, gave them the opportunity to do so, but there you would have a case in which you see a certain merging of large-scale violence from bottom down with top -- top-down decisions or bottom-up and top-down decisions. Did I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think you, in a sense, address this a little bit later, in the next section or the next section but one, where we look at how these processes develop. The summary of the passage you've just been dealing with, the third conclusion, says that: "In the course of the crisis, a radical and ruthless political elite may succeed in taking over the state organisation. Political behaviours and decisions of this leadership may be considered of decisive importance for the emergence of genocide. It has been argued that a genocidal process does not develop from bottom up but is typically top down although the precise involvement of the state may take different forms. One corollary is that the highest state authorities are always responsible for what happens during the genocidal process." And then this: "Another corollary" - perhaps you'd just comment on this last sentence and then we'll move on - "another corollary implies that single acts of genocide should be considered against the background of the prevalent power and authority structure within the state society concerned." And it may be that that sentence can also connect to His Honour's question. I'm not sure but could you amplify --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly can. I'm convinced when you look at single separate or isolated events during genocidal process that you will have to -- if you want to understand these separate events, you will have to connect them to a larger view of the power structure within the society concerned, because many people on local and regional levels, for instance, will only act in a violent way when they can be more or less sure that they can get away with it and that they got some impunity. So that's maybe --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Part 5 of your report between pages 21 and 26 is headed, "The process of genocide, planning and the division of labour." It's largely self-explanatory, and I don't need to ask you any questions about it but one or couple -- save for two. At page 24, at the top of page 24 - again this may, may a matter for you reflect back to His Honour's question - line 3, you speak of genocides gathering speed like flywheels, and that's a picturesque way of putting things. A sentence of amplification.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, I -- I used that image to convey the message that if you look at the genocidal process and you look at the first phase or the initial phase, you will usually find all sorts of obstacles or barriers before getting it launched. It might be a very general decision of central political authority to do away with such or such a category of people, but then still the whole planning still has been -- has to be done. Practical and realistic particular plans have to be drawn up, and that will mean that initially a genocidal process will take time, energy, investments to get going, but once it is organised and once it is running, it might gather speed like a flywheel in the sense that it will be running smoothly after some time and become routinised and it will -- people will learn by doing, perpetrators will learn by doing, and they will find ways and means to go on with genocidal campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then following from that, the first two lines of paragraph 39 and remembering that you said that there's no suggestion that these events occur naturally in societies, or civilised societies, well, any societies, you say that once under way they seldom or never be stopped by the same people who set them in motion. This is your flywheel?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's partly my flywheel, but it's also what has been said under paragraph 38, that when people become involved in genocidal crimes or mass crimes targeting specific groups, they will become involved in a criminal career, and it's not usual for people who get into such a career to have any further recourse to the law or to formal authority. So it will be very difficult once they get in to stop, because they have to cover up all the time what they have been doing, and they're connected to each other also.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your conclusion, the fourth conclusion, puts it in a slightly different way. It says that these events are usually -- the conclusion of such events are usually brought about by forceful external intervention. In any of the large events that you've particularly focused on, has there been a process of natural cessation or has there always been --

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: No. In the four cases I have used as examples in this report, they were all stopped from the outside by military intervention in different ways, but it was never stopped by the perpetrators themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at page 25 of the same section, paragraph 40 and then a line from 42, you make the point in paragraph 40 that within the division of labour you've covered in this part of your report, leadership characteristically does or does not make detailed decisions about the genocidal or similar process?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: The top leadership usually only makes very general decisions and thereby gives other people the means and the organisation and sometimes also the money and the armed force to organise the process in a more detailed way, in a more realistic way. We know, for instance, that Hitler, to give that example, never witnessed any genocidal acts himself, nor did he ever write down an order "kill all Jews," but we can be very certain especially in discussions with Himmler and others, that he must have stated the order, that is "kill all the Jews."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that -- that is famous example -- or very famous exam. Is there a reflection of that in the other of the cases you've studied?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Certainly. The facts are often difficult to ascertain, but we know, for instance, that three main leaders of the Ottoman Empire at the beginning of the First World War have decided that the Turkish state would do away with the Armenian minority and also with a large part of the Greek minority in Anatolia. Very often the evidence is circumstantial. Maybe I could add that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then at paragraph 42 of your report, the foot of the page, 25 and over to page 26, you make the point that the leadership, unlike the lower-level perpetrators, typically are unlikely to be caught red-handed or apprehended at all.

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, the top leadership, at least as far as I know, very often are aware of the extremist character of their decisions, and so they don't leave traces usually. We don't have written orders in these different cases that such-and-such category of people should become the victim of a genocidal process. That's one of the reasons. One of the other reasons is that in several cases, as you all know in Cambodia, for instance, or in Indonesia in 1965, no process ever followed the happening of a genocidal campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally from the report and then one last question and I'm done, but finally from the report, part 6 which is headed Genocidal Crimes and Ideology, and which goes from page 26 to 31, nothing from the report itself but drawing on that section of the report, what can you tell us, please, about the significance of societies being divided in some way before these crimes can be committed, about the use of propaganda, and indeed about the perpetrating group casting itself as victim?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Well, a fundamental precondition for a genocidal process in a society is that there are some divisions within the population. These might be of an ethnic nature or a religious nature or a majority/minority, but there should be some divisions. Now, at a certain point in time, for instance by a radical elite, these divisions might become a main point in an ideological stance which might argue as follow -- as follows: We are threatened. We the national majority, for instance, are threatened by certain minorities or other groups. They do not belong to our nation. They should be excluded. And in its most radical form, the conclusion might be they should be ousted of our country or killed. And I think that's where ideology fulfils a very important function and will also be actively used in propaganda to convince part of the population, part of the perpetrators, to act with violence against an innocent minority, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Incidentally going back to His Honour Judge Robinson's question, and paragraph 54 perhaps can pick up on this, although there can be this consequence of a "top down" approach, others may, of course, be driven not by those motives at all but might have entirely selfish objectives in the crimes they commit. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's certainly correct. Research has shown that participants in the perpetration of genocidal crimes harbour all sorts of different motivations. Some might be devoted nationalists or devoted national socialists, for instance in the German case. In other cases, people might just be out for looting or plundering or money income. People might want to make a career. But apart from these individual motivations, I would emphasise, if I may, that the ideology gives a sort of overall sense of direction to what should be done and imparts a sense of purpose and intent to all the individual perpetrators apart from their personal individual motivations which may be quite variated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the creation of a them and us culture characteristic, essential, or what?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. It's very important. It's very important that the people of which the perpetrator wants to get rid are seen as "them" and not "us." That's also connected in a dehumanising tendency to exclude certain people from, let's say, the common universe of human obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the need for dehumanisation or the incidence of dehumanisation in all those cases you've studied?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: They illustrate all the time the same mechanism between "them" and "us," but it also makes clear, I think, that a certain degree of dehumanisation is a precondition for large-scale killing. It's not so very easy for people to kill on a large scale, so they have to be convinced that those they are killing are evil and less than human, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then within the general heading of Propaganda, probably my penultimate question: Is the collective historical memory of any part of a them-and-us culture of any significance?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: Yes. That depends on the case at which you're looking, but to give a few examples, I think for the genocidal process against the Jews, the very widespread antisemitism was a very important condition. Many Germans already believed that Jews were evil and conspiring against the German nation. In cases of Hutus and Tutsis, perhaps I can give that example too from Rwanda, Hutus saw themselves, and also with some ground, as victims of Tutsi supremacy for a long time. So in 1994, the organising perpetrators could make use of collective memories among Hutus, collective memories as victims and might turn that experience into a perpetrator's wish to end the victimised status.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Literally two last questions. It may be typically the them-and-us culture is a bipartite thing. Would your conclusions be any different if you were dealing not with a bipartite but a three-party or a four-party them-and-us culture?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: It would complicate the research questions, but I think you would find similar mechanisms but in a more complicated way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then outside your report but something that I wish you to help us with, incidents of people characterised as perpetrators doing some good to those characterised as victims, is that a feature, a common feature or an exception in the studies you've done?

utterances.speaker: TON ZWAAN
utterances.text: If I understand you well, you will find such cases, and even in nearly every case you study. And that also has some reasons. Perpetrators might realise what they are doing and might, so to speak, try to make some capital for later on by, for instance, protecting certain families out of the victim category or certain groups. And in all the cases I know of, there are examples of such behaviour. So perpetrators might be large-scale killers or organisers of large-scale killings and at the same time protect a handful of victims out of the same category.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment while we consider tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For time tomorrow we have in mind one hour and a half, the first hearing, for this. If you have some point, a useful point, if you're going to argue for more time, it is open to you, but at the moment you have an hour and a half, and we do not at the moment intend to increase that. But it's -- if you wish to argue, then you can do that. That's tomorrow. Mr. Zwaan, thank you very much for coming. Please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. Could you be back again at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn now until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of January, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
